title: Organic farming — FAO
question: What is organic farming?
content: Organic farming is a farming system that supports soil organisms, biodiversity and natural biological cycles. It uses locally adapted practices such as crop rotation and biological or mechanical management, with restrictions on synthetic inputs. Simply avoiding synthetic inputs does not by itself establish organic certification.

title: Crop rotation — FAO
question: What is crop rotation?
content: Crop rotation is growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same field over successive seasons or years. It can help maintain soil fertility and reduce the pest, disease and weed problems associated with repeatedly growing the same crop.

title: Drip irrigation — FAO
question: What is drip irrigation?
content: Drip irrigation is a method that delivers water slowly through small emitters near plants, wetting part of the root zone. Good management can reduce runoff, deep drainage and evaporation losses. The crop still needs its full water requirement; the irrigation method does not reduce that requirement.

title: Blocked drip emitters — FAO
question: Why do drip irrigation emitters become blocked?
content: Drip emitters can become blocked by sediment, algae or mineral and fertilizer deposits. Filtration helps remove suspended material, but some chemical blockage problems need advice from the equipment supplier or an irrigation specialist.

title: Compost and composting — FAO
question: What is compost?
content: Compost is decomposed organic material produced through managed microbial breakdown of materials such as crop residues and animal wastes. Composting turns suitable organic residues into a soil amendment that supplies organic matter and nutrients and can improve soil properties.

title: Plant-residue mulching — FAO TECA
question: What is mulching?
content: Mulching is covering the soil surface with material such as straw, leaves or crop residues. Plant-residue mulch supports soil organisms, helps water enter the soil and protects against erosion. As organic mulch decomposes, it contributes organic matter to the soil.

title: Integrated pest management — FAO
question: What is integrated pest management?
content: Integrated pest management is an approach that combines suitable biological, cultural, physical and chemical methods to manage pests. IPM aims to grow healthy crops while reducing unnecessary pesticide use and risks to people and the environment, and supporting natural pest-control processes.
scope: general education; no pesticide dosage recommendation

title: Soil health — USDA NRCS
question: What is soil health?
content: Soil health is the ability of soil to keep functioning as a living system that supports plants, animals and people. Healthy soil supports nutrient cycling, water storage and the organisms that contribute to productive ecosystems.

title: Improving soil health — USDA NRCS
question: How can I improve soil health?
content: To improve soil health, reduce unnecessary soil disturbance, keep the soil covered, grow a diversity of crops, and maintain living roots for more of the year. Practices such as cover crops and diverse rotations can improve organic matter, water infiltration and nutrient cycling.

title: Cover crops — USDA NRCS
question: What are cover crops?
content: Cover crops are crops grown to protect and improve soil during periods when it would otherwise be bare. They can reduce erosion and nutrient losses, improve water infiltration and organic matter, suppress weeds and provide habitat for useful organisms.

title: Green manure — FAO
question: What is green manure?
content: Green manure is a crop grown so its fresh plant material can be incorporated into the soil to add organic matter. Cover crops may use the same species, but their defining purpose is to cover and protect the soil rather than necessarily being incorporated.

title: Soil testing — Government of India Soil Health Card programme
question: Why should I test my soil?
content: Soil testing measures soil properties and nutrient status to guide crop-specific fertilizer and soil-amendment decisions. The Soil Health Card programme reports information such as pH, electrical conductivity, organic carbon and nutrient levels, with recommendations based on the test results.
scope: general education; no field-specific fertilizer dose

title: Soil Health Card — Government of India
question: What is a Soil Health Card?
content: A Soil Health Card is a report of a farm's soil test results. It describes nutrient status and other measured soil properties and provides crop-based fertilizer and soil-improvement recommendations. It helps farmers use the actual condition of their soil when planning nutrient management.

title: Vasantrao Naik Marathwada Krishi Vidyapeeth — official university information
question: What is VNMKV?
aliases: વી એન એમ કે વી શું છે
content: VNMKV stands for Vasantrao Naik Marathwada Krishi Vidyapeeth, an agricultural university in Parbhani, Maharashtra, established in 1972. Its work includes agricultural education, research based on regional needs and extension activities that share farming knowledge and technology.

title: MahaDBT farm mechanization document checklist — official scheme page

title: Intercropping — FAO AGROVOC
question: What is intercropping?
aliases: two crops same field at same time
content: Intercropping means cultivating two or more crops together in one field during the same period. Crop rotation instead places different crops in a sequence over time.

title: Water harvesting for crops — FAO
question: What is rainwater harvesting in farming?
content: Water harvesting is collecting rainfall runoff for later or targeted use, such as directing it into crop-growing soil or storing it in a tank or farm reservoir for supplementary irrigation. Planning depends on rainfall, the catchment area, storage capacity and crop water needs.

title: Agroforestry — FAO
question: What is agroforestry?
content: Agroforestry is a farming system that integrates trees or shrubs with crops, pasture or livestock. Alley cropping is one form, with crops grown between rows of woody plants. The design must fit local soil, water, climate and crop conditions.
